content: Mineral water is a type of water that contains minerals or other dissolved substances, which can influence its taste or provide therapeutic benefits. These dissolved substances may include salts, sulfur compounds, and gases. Mineral water is often naturally effervescent due to the presence of dissolved gases. Mineral water can either occur naturally or be artificially prepared. Historically, people would consume or use mineral water directly at its source, a practice often referred to as taking the waters or taking the cure. Locations where this occurred were commonly known as spas, baths, or wells. The term spa was used when the water was both consumed and used for bathing, bath referred to locations where the water was primarily used for bathing, and well referred to sites where the water was mainly consumed but not used for bathing. In many cases, these mineral water sites became popular tourist destinations, even in ancient times, as seen in places like Bath, England. This led to the development of spa towns and hydropathic hotels, often referred to as Hydros. In modern times, it is far more common for mineral water to be bottled directly at the source for widespread distribution and consumption. Visiting the original mineral water site to access the water directly has become rare and, in many cases, is no longer possible due to exclusive commercial ownership rights. Globally, there are over 3,000 commercially available brands of mineral water. According to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), mineral water is defined as water that contains at least 250 parts per million (ppm) of total dissolved solids (TDS). It must originate from a geologically and physically protected underground water source, accessed through one or more boreholes or springs. Importantly, no additional minerals may be added to water classified as mineral water.
